papers.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
papers.abstract: Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

papers.title: Longitudinal persistence of EEG brain fingerprints: phase and complex coherency geometry across sessions and functional states
papers.abstract: Sensor-level EEG coherency can distinguish individuals, although its phase and magnitude patterns may reflect neural activity, source mixing, and recording geometry. We evaluated two geometric representations of complex coherency - unit phasors and full complex coherency - alongside triangle holonomies and magnitude-only descriptors. Using direct enrollment-probe matching without a trained identity classifier, we analyzed three independent longitudinal cohorts: RestCog (N = 60; approximately one month), L-FAME (N = 44; six weeks), and Dortmund (N = 206; approximately five years). In eyes-closed rest-to-rest matching, alpha phasors identified 81.67% of participants in RestCog (AUC 0.9473) and 79.55% in L-FAME (AUC 0.9735); full complex coherency identified 78.33% and 84.09%, respectively. After five years in Dortmund, fixed row-standardized alpha-beta fusion yielded 77.67% rank-1 identification (AUC 0.9744) for phasors and 70.39% (AUC 0.9527) for full coherency. Changes in functional state exposed different strengths: full coherency preserved higher rank-1 accuracy in some monthly RestCog rest-to-task comparisons, whereas alpha phasors retained higher verification AUC. Switching between eyes-closed and eyes-open recordings in Dortmund substantially weakened identification with both representations. Triangle holonomies also retained individual information across visits. An exact factorization of complex cosine shows how magnitude-pattern alignment and magnitude-weighted phase agreement contribute to full-coherency matching. Together, the results establish longitudinally discriminative structure in measured scalp EEG coherency over weeks to years, while distinguishing persistence across visits from robustness to changes in recording state.

papers.title: Sleep Renormalizes Negative Emotional Generalization
papers.abstract: Overgeneralization of negative experiences co-occurs with sleep disruption and characterizes anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A strategically-designed behavioral paradigm tested whether sleep shifts emotional generalization away from negative and toward positive representations. Participants learned positive, negative, or neutral face-outcome associations, then completed immediate and delayed generalization testing with morphed faces after sleep or wakefulness. Sleep selectively enhanced positive generalization, whereas wakefulness favored negative generalization. To uncover the underlying neural mechanisms, individual variability in generalization was examined using fMRI and high-density EEG. Amygdala and limbic activity during outcome-processing predicted both stronger immediate negative generalization and a sleep-specific shift toward positive generalization. Additionally, sleep-spindle activity positively correlated with post-sleep increases in positive generalization and reductions in negative generalization. Together, these findings identify a neural mechanism through which sleep reduces negative bias while strengthening positive representations, highlighting a pathway by which sleep may protect against maladaptive generalization associated with anxiety and PTSD.

papers.title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
papers.abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

papers.title: DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 regulates the circadian clock in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: The Arabidopsis transcriptome must be continuously reshaped to integrate endogenous and environmental cues, including the circadian clock and ambient light. This reprogramming relies on the coordinated synthesis and degradation of mRNAs, yet the contribution of RNA decay factors to circadian regulation remains poorly characterized. Here, we show that nearly all core clock genes are high-amplitude clock-controlled genes (HA-CCGs). A meta-analysis of transcriptome-wide mRNA decay datasets revealed that HA-CCGs have consistently shorter half-lives across multiple studies. We further identify the mRNA decapping activator DECAPPING PROTEIN 5 (DCP5) as a key regulator of circadian RNA stability. Using iCLIP, we show that DCP5 binds preferentially to HA-CCG transcripts at AU-rich motifs in their 3' UTRs, thereby modulating their stability. Accordingly, the dcp5 mutant displays an extended circadian period at both physiological and molecular levels. Our findings establish mRNA decay as a post-transcriptional regulatory layer that fine-tunes the decay of multiple key transcripts within the circadian system.

papers.title: No Effect of Exercise Timing on Daily Glycaemia Despite Shifts in Acute Glucose Dynamics in Participants with Normal Glucose Tolerance: A Randomised Crossover Trial
papers.abstract: Exercise is a well-established modulator of glucose regulation, but whether the time of day it is performed matters for healthy, free-living adults remains unresolved. In a randomised crossover trial, 29 healthy adults completed a single 30-minute bout of moderate-intensity exercise in the morning (07:00-10:00) and in the evening (16:00-19:00), with continuous glucose monitoring and wrist-worn activity tracking used to capture responses over an 8-day free-living protocol. Evening exercise produced a significantly greater acute reduction in blood glucose (P < 0.001) compared to morning exercise, but this did not translate into consistent differences in overall daily mean glycaemic exposure, whether measured over the calendar day or over a window aligned with exercise onset. Evening exercise was linked to greater within-day glycaemic variability than morning exercise, with the clearest evidence coming from the circadian-aligned analysis (day x timing interaction, SD: P = 0.00939; CV: P = 0.00766). Appetite rose after exercise in both conditions, with no difference by time of day. Taken together, these results show that exercise timing does not change how much glucose exposure a healthy adult accumulates over a day, but it does change the shape of the glucose response around the exercise bout itself, a distinction only visible when glucose is examined at a finer temporal resolution than daily averages allow.
